principles.heading: A few principles I hold firmly, and apply with judgment.
principles.principle_1.title: My opinion is interesting, but irrelevant.
principles.principle_1.body: Customer evidence decides. I brought direct user discovery to a team that relied on internal stakeholders, with 50+ conversations at eXp. At Virbela, 200+ customer interviews and structured discovery sprints cut wasted engineering effort by 25% in the first year.
principles.principle_2.title: Teams own outcomes, not tickets.
principles.principle_2.body: Each PM gets a business domain, a dedicated team and its own stakeholders, and is accountable for results in that domain.
principles.principle_3.title: Technical health is product work.
principles.principle_3.body: One roadmap, not two. Better testing means fewer defects reach users. Better logging means we tell users about a problem before they tell us. Each year, developers propose a dedicated cleanup cycle for me to review.
principles.principle_4.title: Release early, switch on when ready.
principles.principle_4.body: Features go to production behind flags. When something goes wrong, we turn a flag off instead of rolling back a whole release.
principles.principle_5.title: Measure each team on what matters to its users.
principles.principle_5.body: Our revenue-share team serves a few hundred high-value agents, so it is judged on how well it serves them, not on raw user counts.
principles.principle_6.title: Hire for curiosity. Require only the real deal-breakers.
principles.principle_6.body: One of my best PMs had limited experience and would not have made it past a conventional job description.

lead.coaching.heading: How four analysts became product managers
lead.coaching.intro: The path I used at eXp to take four business analysts to independent product managers who own their domains.
lead.coaching.step_1.title: Give them a domain, not a backlog
lead.coaching.step_1.body: Restructure ownership around a real business area, so each person is accountable for outcomes — not just tickets.
lead.coaching.step_2.title: Teach discovery, not feature intake
lead.coaching.step_2.body: Probe past the requested feature to the underlying workflow, validate with users, and bring that evidence into prioritization.
lead.coaching.step_3.title: Clear the busywork
lead.coaching.step_3.body: Roll out AI-assisted workflows for story writing — ~20 PMs and partners trained — and reinvest the time in customers and stakeholders.
lead.coaching.step_4.title: Hand over the roadmap
lead.coaching.step_4.body: They own discovery, stakeholder relationships, prioritization and delivery for their domain. I move to coach and unblock.
lead.pillar_1.title: Hire
lead.pillar_1.body: I write the job descriptions and make the final call, screening for curiosity and judgment over checklists.
lead.pillar_2.title: Manage
lead.pillar_2.body: Performance reviews, promotion and raise cases, and the hard conversations when they're needed.
lead.pillar_3.title: Develop
lead.pillar_3.body: I took four business analysts to independent product managers, doing more myself early and stepping back as they grew.
lead.pillar_4.title: Organize
lead.pillar_4.body: I give people domains with real ownership instead of routing every decision through me.

stories.heading: What it looks like in practice.
stories.intro: The details of my enterprise work belong to the companies I did it for. Here is what I can share.
stories.story_1.title: Building teams that own their work
stories.story_1.body: At eXp I started with a capable group that had no defined ownership, where every decision routed through me. I designed a pod model: each PM got a dedicated team of developers and QA, a business domain, and that domain’s stakeholders. At Virbela I made a similar change, replacing “whichever team can build it fastest” with joint design across the server, client and web teams.
stories.story_1.outcome: Delivery got faster, stakeholder conflicts were settled inside domains instead of escalating, and My eXp grew beyond its revenue-share origins.
stories.story_2.title: Shipping on a date that couldn’t move
stories.story_2.body: On September 30, 2026, we relaunched My eXp alongside a rebuilt Mira AI copilot. With three weeks left, the app was ahead and Mira was behind. I checked commitments with the other PMs, aligned with the engineering manager, and moved engineers onto Mira, while keeping a tested fallback version ready.
stories.story_2.outcome: Both shipped on the date. The fallback wasn’t needed, and Mira now answers with ~95% measured accuracy.
stories.story_3.title: Retiring legacy systems for 88K users
stories.story_3.body: We rebuilt key legacy functionality inside My eXp, then moved 88K agents over in stages: run both systems in parallel, announce, give formal notice with in-app messaging, then switch off. A rollback plan was ready.
stories.story_4.title: Correcting a number people watched closely
stories.story_4.body: A figure our most engaged users checked often was calculated differently from the way their actual payouts worked. The payouts were always right, but the number on screen wasn’t. I identified the affected users in the data, planned the communication before touching the product, and shipped a transition that showed both numbers.
stories.story_4.cta: There’s more to this one. Happy to walk through it.
